def: A perspective that unites animal liberation with other social liberation struggles (racial, gender, class) under a single political horizon.
com: It reflects the view that speciesism shares structural roots with other forms of oppression, and that fighting them in isolation would be strategically and ethically insufficient.

def: A system of symbolic communication used to represent and convey meaning.
com: Its historical use as a criterion for the moral exclusion of nonhuman animals is criticised by sentientist currents, for which the absence of complex verbal language is irrelevant given the proven capacity to suffer.

def: Forms of communication used by nonhuman animals, such as vocalisations, gestures and chemical signals, studied to understand the cognition of different species.
com: Findings in this area have progressively narrowed the gap that was once assumed to exist between human communication and that of other species.

def: The attitude of forming opinions through reason and evidence, not authority, tradition or dogma.
com: The term arose in England in the late 17th and the 18th century, among critics of religious authority, such as Anthony Collins, author of *A Discourse of Free-Thinking* (1713). Thinking freely helps revise inherited beliefs, including about animals. But it doesn't mean every conclusion is equally good: free thinkers are still bound by the evidence, and the label is sometimes used to reject scientific consensus without good reasons. See Critical thinking, Skepticism and Evidence.

def: The branch of philosophy that studies correct reasoning: when a conclusion follows from the premises.
com: An argument is valid when, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true too; and it is sound when, besides being valid, its premises are actually true. Every chapter of the guide runs this test: it reconstructs the strongest version of the objection and shows whether it fails on validity or on a premise. Logic alone doesn't settle facts or values: it shows what follows from what one accepts, so it needs premises supported by evidence. See Argument, Fallacies, Logical consistency and Evidence.

def: The philosophical position that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time, because the future may last a very long time and hold an immense number of beings.
com: Formulated within effective altruism by philosophers such as William MacAskill, Toby Ord and Nick Bostrom, in practice it focuses mostly on humanity's future, especially on reducing the risks of extinction. Animal advocates argue that the same logic requires including all the sentient beings of the future, most of whom will probably not be human, and draw attention to s-risks. See Effective altruism, S-risks and X-risks.

def: A dietary system of Japanese origin, based on the idea of balance between yin and yang, that prioritizes whole grains, legumes and vegetables; someone who follows it is called macrobiotic.
com: It was popularized in the West in the 20th century by George Ohsawa and Michio Kushi. Many versions are almost plant-based but include fish, so macrobiotics isn't the same as veganism. Very restrictive versions, especially in children, have been linked to nutritional deficiencies, such as of vitamin B12 and vitamin D.

def: A dairy fat obtained by churning cream.
The identification of animals by hot-iron branding, ear tags or other means, usually without anaesthesia.
com: Hot-iron branding burns the skin until it scars and causes intense pain; freeze branding, with an iron chilled in liquid nitrogen, also hurts, though generally less. Other methods include ear notching, as in piglets, ear tags and tattoos. Ear tags and microchips cause less pain and replace branding in many places; in Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule bans ear notching from 2030. See Tabuleta (livestock tag, Brazilian usage), Anesthesia and Physical integrity.

def: A spread made mainly from vegetable oils; many are vegan, but several contain whey, milk powder or vitamin D3 from lanolin, so it is worth reading the label.
A facility where animals are slaughtered for consumption.
com: Slaughterhouses run fast lines, with thousands of birds per hour, which makes it hard to correct stunning failures. They are generally closed to the public, which keeps slaughter out of consumers' sight. The work has high injury rates, and research points to psychological effects on workers; a 2009 study by Amy Fitzgerald and colleagues found in the United States an association between the presence of slaughterhouses and higher rates of some crimes, without establishing causation. See Slaughter, Stunning of animals and Humane slaughter.

def: A decision principle that prescribes choosing the course of action in which the well-being of the worst-off is as high as possible, regardless of the total or average sum of well-being.
com: In contexts of animal exploitation, this principle would favour prioritising the reduction of suffering of the worst-off individuals (often animals in extreme confinement), even when this does not maximise aggregate well-being.

def: The central principle of utilitarianism, according to which the right action is the one that produces the greatest possible balance of well-being over suffering.
com: Applied consistently, this principle requires counting the suffering and well-being of all sentient beings affected by an action, not only humans.

def: A decision principle under uncertainty that weighs possible outcomes by their probability.
com: In contexts of uncertainty about the sentience of a given species, this principle can justify moral caution: even a moderate probability of sentience is enough to recommend avoiding harm to it.

def: A sugary substance produced by bees from flower nectar; strict veganism rejects its consumption because it involves the exploitation of insects.
com: In commercial beekeeping, common practices include clipping the queen's wings, artificially inseminating her, replacing her periodically and replacing the honey taken with sugar syrup. Research by Lars Chittka's group in London suggests that bees may have some form of subjective experience, although the question remains open. Some vegans disagree about honey because of this uncertainty, but the Vegan Society's position is that it is not vegan. See Beekeeping, Propolis and Insectivory.

def: Alternative techniques to animal experimentation (cell cultures, computer models) developed under the principle of the 3Rs.
com: They include human cell and tissue cultures, organs-on-chips, computer models and studies with human volunteers at safe doses. In 2022 a US law, the FDA Modernization Act 2.0, removed the legal requirement for animal tests to approve new drugs, without banning them, and in 2025 the FDA announced a plan to reduce these tests, starting with monoclonal antibodies. In Brazil, CONCEA, the federal council that regulates animal use in research, recognizes validated alternative methods and sets deadlines for their adoption. Even so, validated methods replace only part of the tests, and validation tends to be slow. See 3Rs, Animal experimentation and Arouca Law.

def: Active and organised engagement in defence of a political or social cause, including the animal cause.
A group that, for numerical or power-related reasons, has less social influence; a concept used by analogy to discuss the political position of animals as a group without its own representation.
The use of an animal (usually a horse) to be ridden by humans.
An internal factor, psychological, ethical or biological, that drives an agent to act in a certain way.
com: In the case of adopting veganism, the literature on behaviour change suggests that ethical motivations, centred on the interests of animals, tend to be more stable over time than motivations centred exclusively on health or appearance.

def: Organised collective action sustained over time, aimed at promoting or resisting social change; a category that includes the animal advocacy movement.
The set of individuals, groups and organisations that promote veganism as a philosophy and social practice.
A profound transformation in how a society or field of knowledge understands a given subject, such as the growing acceptance of animal sentience.
The surgical removal of skin around the tail of sheep (usually without anaesthesia) to prevent infestation by fly larvae, a common practice in wool production.
com: It is done mainly in Australia, on merino lambs, with shears, and for a long time without any pain relief. New Zealand banned the practice in 2018, and the Australian state of Victoria now requires pain relief; retailers and fashion brands in several countries refuse wool from mulesed sheep. The alternative advocated by veterinarians and animal protection organizations is to breed sheep with fewer skin folds, which are less susceptible to flystrike. See Wool, Anesthesia and Artificial selection.

def: An ethical and political principle of rejecting violence as a means of action, historically associated with traditions such as Jainism and Hinduism (ahimsa) and with pacifist social movements, including strands of animal activism.
com: Extending this principle to animals implies recognising that causing them avoidable harm, and not only humans, is morally equivalent to an act of violence.

def: What a being needs to live well; in ethics, the criterion that separates unavoidable harm from avoidable harm.
com: In biology, an animal's needs include food, shelter, movement, companionship and the expression of natural behaviors, and being deprived of them causes suffering. In ethics, almost everyone and many laws accept that causing unnecessary suffering is wrong; the debate is about what counts as necessary. For most people with access to varied food, eating animals isn't necessary for health, according to nutrition bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. See the argument "Eating animals is necessary to survive".

def: An automatic physiological response to harmful stimuli, distinct from conscious pain; a point of debate in species such as fish and invertebrates.
com: Sentientist currents hold that, where there is uncertainty about whether nociception is accompanied by conscious experience in a given species, the benefit of the doubt should favour the animal rather than the practice that exploits it.

def: A term coined by the jurist Gary Francione for organisations that claim animal rights as their goal but advocate welfare reforms as a step.
com: It is used critically by abolitionists. Pragmatists reject the label and say the reforms are steps towards ending exploitation.

def: The science that studies the processes by which organisms obtain and use food; central to discussions about the viability of plant-based diets.
com: Nutrition bodies have progressively recognised that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can be nutritionally adequate at all stages of life, which weakens the nutritional argument traditionally used against veganism.

def: A medical specialty (recognised in Brazil) dedicated to the diagnosis and treatment of nutritional issues in humans, relevant to debates about health on vegan diets.
com: (see the note under Nutrition)

def: The position that there are moral truths that are valid independently of opinion or culture.
com: If objective moral truths exist, and if the capacity to suffer is morally relevant, it follows that excluding animals from moral consideration would be objectively unjustified, and not a mere matter of cultural preference.

def: Failing to act when action would be possible; discussed in terms of moral responsibility for harms not prevented.
com: In the case of wild animals, more radical sentientist currents argue that omission in the face of avoidable suffering in nature may also be morally questionable, one of the most controversial topics in contemporary animal ethics. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022), drawing on the equivalence thesis, defended by James Rachels and, with qualifications, by Peter Singer, argues that allowing a harm we could prevent is not, in itself, less serious than causing it, while much of deontology, with Philippa Foot and Warren Quinn, holds that doing is worse than allowing. This is the subject of the argument "We didn't cause it, so we have no duty to help". See Equivalence thesis, Positive and negative duties, Natural harms and Wild animal suffering.

def: A diet that includes both plant and animal foods; in biology, a trait of animals such as humans, pigs, bears and rats.
com: Being biologically omnivorous means being able to digest both kinds of food, not needing to eat animals: a well-planned plant-based diet meets human needs. Concluding that we should eat animals because we can is the naturalistic fallacy. See Herbivory, Carnivorism and Vegan diet.

def: The systematic exercise of power that subordinates and harms a group.
com: Its application, by analogy, to the treatment of animals within social and economic structures is central to the currents that describe speciesism as a form of structural oppression, comparable, with due differences taken into account, to other forms of domination.

def: Vegetarianism that includes eggs and dairy but excludes all meat, including fish and seafood.
com: It is the most common form of vegetarianism in the West. Eggs and milk don't require killing the animal at the time of consumption, but the industries that produce them do kill: in egg production, billions of male chicks are killed at birth, and hens and cows are slaughtered when production falls; in dairy, calves are separated from their mothers. See Ovo-vegetarianism and Lacto-vegetarianism.

def: Vegetarianism that includes eggs but excludes dairy and all meat.
com: It is sometimes adopted because of lactose intolerance or objection to the dairy industry. Commercial egg production, however, also involves killing male chicks and slaughtering hens when laying declines. See Lacto-ovo vegetarianism.

def: A figure of speech that combines contradictory terms.
com: Expressions such as "humane slaughter" or "happy meat" are described this way by antispeciesists, who consider it incompatible to cause the death of a being that wants to live with any notion of genuine humaneness or happiness for that being.

def: A being that can be morally affected, benefited or harmed, even without being a moral agent.
com: Nonhuman animals fall into this category: even though they cannot be held responsible for their actions, they have interests whose violation or promotion is morally relevant.

def: The set of food preferences formed in childhood, relevant to discussions about food education and the transition to plant-based diets.
The breeding and use of animals for economic purposes, mainly food.
com: It is one part of agriculture and livestock farming (agropecuária), along with crop farming. Veganism opposes livestock farming, not crop farming.

def: Raising animals over large areas, at lower animal density.
com: Animals generally have more space and can express more natural behaviours, but they still go through castration, branding, transport and slaughter, and are more exposed to heat, cold and predators. Because it uses a lot of land, extensive cattle ranching is the main cause of deforestation in Brazil, especially in the Amazon, according to analyses compiled by Our World in Data. See Intensive livestock farming, Agribusiness and Extinction.

def: A small-scale model, usually for subsistence or the local market.
An industrial-scale model, oriented towards maximum productivity and lowest cost.
com: It is the dominant model in global production of chicken, eggs and pork. Its low costs depend partly on externalities that do not appear in the price, such as water and air pollution from manure, heavy antibiotic use, the risk of new diseases and the animals' suffering. See Animal confinement, Externality and Antimicrobial resistance.

def: Raising animals at high density with heavy use of inputs and technology.
A model of animal farming that seeks to reduce environmental impacts and increase resource efficiency, without necessarily changing the paradigm of using animals as a resource.
com: Measures such as improving pastures, reducing losses and using feed additives can lower emissions per kilogram of meat or milk. Even so, a 2018 study by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek, which analysed about 38,000 farms in 119 countries, concluded that the lowest-impact animal products typically exceed the impacts of plant-based substitutes. The term also says nothing about the animals' welfare or their death. See Livestock farming, Sentientist environmentalism and Plant protein.

def: A genealogical record that documents an animal's lineage, used for selective breeding.
com: Pedigree breeding selects animals for the appearance set out in breed standards, which has concentrated hereditary diseases in many breeds, such as breathing problems in short-nosed dogs like bulldogs and pugs. The BBC documentary *Pedigree Dogs Exposed* (2008) led to revisions of breed standards in the United Kingdom and to the BBC dropping its coverage of the Crufts show. From a sentientist point of view, the criticism goes beyond health: commercial breeding of purebred animals continues while shelters are full. See Artificial selection, Pet shop and Adoption.

def: Industries producing animal fur and leather, with specific debates about suffering and synthetic alternatives.
com: Animal protection organizations estimate that about 100 million animals, mainly mink and foxes, are killed each year for fur, most of them raised in wire cages. Several countries have banned fur farming, such as the United Kingdom, in 2000, Austria, Norway and the Netherlands, and many fashion brands have stopped using fur. Leather is often seen as a mere by-product of meat, but it is a co-product that generates revenue for the livestock industry, and chrome tanning can pollute rivers and harm workers' health. See Wool, Silk and Livestock farming.

def: The ability to evaluate claims and arguments carefully: identifying premises, weighing evidence, recognizing fallacies and biases, and reaching conclusions proportionate to the reasons.
com: It isn't the same as distrusting everything or disagreeing on principle; it includes knowing when to trust experts and changing one's mind in the face of good reasons. Its hardest test is applying it to one's own beliefs, not just to other people's. In the debate about animals, it helps spot appeals to tradition, nature and convenience, but it cuts both ways: a good argument for animals also has to withstand critical scrutiny. See Free thought, Skepticism, Logic and Evidence.

def: In animal ethics and law, the set of psychological characteristics (temperament, preferences, behaviour) that distinguish one individual from another; also used in the legal debate on personhood and legal personality.
com: Recognising legal personality for nonhuman animals is defended by antispeciesist jurists as a way of breaking with the status of mere property to which they are reduced in most legal systems.

def: A debate about recognising animals as subjects of rights, and not merely property. It is defended by antispeciesist jurists as a necessary paradigm shift to break with the historical reduction of animals to the status of property.
The capture of aquatic animals, with a growing debate about fish sentience.
com: In number of individuals, it is the largest form of vertebrate killing: estimates by Alison Mood and Phil Brooke indicate more than a trillion wild fish caught each year. Fish die by suffocation, crushing or decompression, usually without any stunning, and fishing also catches other animals unintentionally, such as turtles, dolphins and birds. There is growing evidence that fish feel pain. See Industrial fishing, Catch and release and Aquaculture.

def: Large-scale fishing, associated with overexploitation and mass suffering.
com: The FAO estimated that 37.7% of assessed fish stocks were overfished in 2021, compared with 10% in 1974. Trawl nets and longlines also catch non-target animals, such as turtles, dolphins, sharks and seabirds, many of them thrown back dead. The fish caught die by asphyxiation, crushing or decompression, without stunning. See Fishing, Aquaculture and Seafood.

def: A diet that excludes the meat of land animals but includes fish and seafood.
com: It isn't a form of vegetarianism, though it is sometimes called one. Fish are sentient, and fishing kills more animals than any other human activity: fishcount estimates put the number of wild fish caught each year at over a trillion. See Vegetarianism.

def: A commercial establishment that sells companion animals and related products.
com: Selling puppies and kittens in shops is criticized for encouraging large-scale commercial breeding, sometimes in poor conditions, while shelters have animals waiting for adoption. Since 2019 California has only allowed shops to offer dogs, cats and rabbits from shelters or rescues, and in 2020 England banned third-party sales of puppies and kittens. Shops also sell birds, fish and reptiles, some captured from the wild. See Breeding facility (criadouro), Adoption and Animal trafficking.

def: The raising of fish in captivity for commercial purposes.
A term for a diet of plant origin, distinct from veganism in that it does not necessarily cover ethics or other uses of animals.
com: The term is attributed to the American biochemist T. Colin Campbell, in the 1980s, as a way to talk about diet without getting into ethics. On a label, "plant-based" does not guarantee that a product is vegan, and companies that sell animal products use the term to attract another audience. See Veganism, Vegan diet and Vegan washing.

def: The name activists give to the restraint structure used to immobilize females during forced mating or artificial insemination.
com: The livestock industry and veterinarians call structures of this kind a restraint chute (tronco de contenção) or brete (see those entries).

def: The position that several ethical theories capture partial truths, with none of them being sufficient on its own.
com: A pluralist can recognise, for example, both the relevance of the total sum of well-being and the importance of prioritising the worst-off, without committing exclusively to a single theory.

def: The extension of moral concern to future generations of animals, at the intersection of animal ethics and longtermism.
A philosophical current that questions anthropocentrism and the centrality of the human as the measure of all things, opening space to reconsider the moral status of animals and other entities.
com: By destabilising the privileged position of the human in the hierarchy of value, it creates relevant philosophical bridges with antispeciesism, although not every posthumanist strand treats animal ethics as a central priority.

def: A social and legal category that lowers the moral status of certain animals (rats, pigeons, insects) because of conflict with human interests.
com: The same animal can be a pest, food, a pet or a protected species, depending on the place and on who is looking: rats are fought in the New York subway, revered at a temple in India and kept as companions in many homes. The science journalist Bethany Brookshire defends this thesis in the book *Pests: How Humans Create Animal Villains* (2022): "pest" is a human label, applied to animals we fear, that thrive in niches we create or that threaten our control over space. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in *Purity and Danger: An Analysis of Concepts of Pollution and Taboo* (1966), described dirt as "matter out of place", something that disturbs an order of classification; the idea helps explain why animals seen as out of place, such as a rat in the kitchen or a pigeon in the square, come to be treated as contamination. From an antispeciesist point of view, the label does not change the animal's capacity to feel, and real conflicts can be handled with prevention, sealing entry points, waste management and non-lethal methods, leaving killing, when unavoidable, to the methods that cause the least suffering. See Synanthropic animals, Animal population control and Invasive alien species.

def: In this context, an approach that prioritises practical and effective results over doctrinal purity in animal advocacy strategies.
com: It is often invoked by reformist and welfarist currents as a strategic justification, and questioned by abolitionists, who see a risk that the pursuit of immediate results legitimises continued forms of exploitation.

def: A pleasant subjective experience; the counterpart of pain in hedonic assessments of well-being.
The property of moral judgements of not only describing but also guiding and requiring a certain action from those who accept them.
com: Recognising animal suffering as morally relevant implies, under this property of moral judgements, a duty to act, and not only an intellectual acknowledgement.

def: A variant that attributes greater value to improvements in the well-being of the worst-off, without requiring strict equality between individuals.
com: By giving extra weight to the suffering of those who are worse off, prioritarianism tends to prioritise interventions that relieve the most intense forms of animal exploitation, even when they do not produce the greatest possible aggregate gain.

def: A political and social stance in favour of change and reform, associated with greater openness to expanding rights and moral consideration to new groups.
com: The inclusion of animals in the progressive agenda is, however, still less consensual than that of other historically marginalised groups, which reflects the persistence of speciesism even in politically progressive sectors.

def: The idea that humanity can expand and refine its ethical judgements over time, as in the historical widening of the moral circle.
com: For antispeciesism, overcoming speciesism represents the next frontier of this progress, historically comparable to the abolition of slavery and the winning of civil rights.

def: A change in the norms and institutions of a society towards greater justice and collective well-being.
com: The growing social acceptance of veganism and animal protection is often interpreted, by advocates of the cause, as part of this process.

def: A resinous substance produced by bees, used for medicinal and cosmetic purposes.
com: Like honey and wax, propolis comes from the hive, so it falls under the same debate about the exploitation of bees; it appears in syrups, sprays and cosmetics sold as natural. See Honey and Beekeeping.

def: The act of actively trying to convince other people to adopt a belief or practice, such as veganism; a term sometimes used pejoratively to criticise approaches seen as aggressive.
com: Activists argue that seeking to persuade others is a natural and legitimate consequence of recognising an ongoing injustice, as happened in other historical social movements.

def: Protein derived from animal tissues or secretions, distinct from plant protein in amino acid composition.
com: It is common to hear that plant protein is "incomplete" and that foods must be combined in the same meal. The 2016 position of the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics is that a variety of plant foods eaten over the course of the day supplies all the essential amino acids, without the need to combine them at each meal. Rice and beans, a common dish in Brazil, is an example of such a combination. See Plant protein, Nutrition and Vegan diet.

def: Protein extracted from the soybean, the basis of various meat substitutes.
A highly concentrated and purified form of soy protein, used industrially in vegan products.
Protein derived from plant sources (legumes, cereals, seeds), a nutritional alternative to animal protein.
Soy protein (or another legume) processed to obtain a fibrous, meat-like texture.
A collective public demonstration of disagreement, used as a tool of animal activism to press for change.
A term used for primitive or partial forms of vegetarianism, generally motivated by practical or cultural reasons more than ethical ones.
A current, practice or discourse that presents itself as veganism but does not start from respect for animals or from the refusal to exploit them, the premises of the term's original definition.
com: On this view, avoiding animal products only for health, for fear of divine punishment, for the environment or as a business strategy, with no link to animal ethics, is strict vegetarianism or a plant-based diet, not veganism. The position rests on the history of the word: in 1949, Leslie Cross, of the Vegan Society, proposed defining veganism as the principle of the emancipation of animals from exploitation by humans, and the definition the society has used since 1988, with small changes in wording, speaks of excluding, as far as is possible and practicable, all forms of exploitation of, and cruelty to, animals. But the usage is disputed: in everyday language, in commerce and in many studies, vegan names the diet or the product, whatever the motive, and many people start for health or the environment and later come to the ethical reason. So the term works better for separating diet from the ethical position than for disqualifying people, and it should not be confused with the speciesist vegan, who refuses animal exploitation but still discriminates by species. See Speciesist vegan, Plant-based, Strict vegetarianism, Eco-veganism and Vegan washing.

def: A set of claims presented as scientific without following the scientific method.
com: Both unfounded claims against the nutritional viability of veganism and exaggerated claims about its benefits can qualify as pseudoscience when not backed by robust evidence.

def: A dairy product obtained by coagulating milk, traditionally using rennet of animal origin.
A substitute for traditional cheese made from nuts, soy or starches, without the use of animal milk.
Industrially manufactured food formulated for farm or companion animals.
Feed formulated without ingredients of animal origin, generally intended for dogs and cats.
com: Dogs are omnivores and, according to the available studies, can do well on nutritionally complete vegan foods; cats are obligate carnivores, but what they need are nutrients, such as taurine, arachidonic acid and vitamin A, which can be synthesized and added to the food. Studies are still few and largely based on guardian reports, such as those by Andrew Knight and colleagues in 2022 and 2023, which found no worse health outcomes in animals on vegan diets. Veterinary associations, such as the British BVA, are more cautious and warn of the risk of poorly formulated diets; the common recommendation is to use foods formulated to be complete and to have the animal followed by a veterinarian. See Animal nutrition, Veterinary ethics and Predation.

def: The capacity to reason logically.
com: Its historical use as a criterion for the moral exclusion of animals is challenged by the argument from marginal cases: humans without full rational capacity, such as babies or people with certain disabilities, are still recognised as deserving moral consideration, which shows that rationality is not in fact the criterion actually applied.

def: A stance that seeks deep changes, going to the root of a problem, rather than superficial adjustments.
com: The word comes from the Latin *radix*, "root". That's why radical doesn't mean violent or extremist, though the words are often used as synonyms: radical concerns the depth of the change advocated, while extremism generally concerns methods and the rejection of pluralism and of others' rights. Many ideas considered radical in their time became consensus, such as the end of slavery and women's suffrage. In the animal movement, radicalism is associated above all with abolitionism, which advocates ending the use of animals as property, not just reforms. A position can be radical in its aim and moderate in tone and means. See Extremism, Abolitionism and Reformism.

def: A stance of opposition to social change, seeking a return to earlier norms or practices.
com: Applied to the animal question, it often relies on appeals to tradition and naturalness, both considered fallacies when used alone as a moral justification.

def: A commitment to reduce, without necessarily eliminating, the consumption of meat, dairy, eggs and other animal products.
com: The term was coined by Brian Kateman, founder of the Reducetarian Foundation in the United States. The idea is that many people reducing has a large effect, and that reducing is easier to start than eliminating. From the animals' point of view, every reduction counts; ethically, reducing is a path, not a destination. See Flexitarianism and Veganism.

def: Gradual and partial changes in the conditions of animal exploitation, promoted by reformist currents as a step towards (or a substitute for) deeper change.
com: Examples are the European Union ban on battery cages for hens, in force since 2012, and the ban on veal crates. The debate is whether these changes pave the way to ending exploitation or make it more acceptable to the public; evidence on this effect is still limited. See Welfarism, Reformism and Moral gradualism.

def: A current that accepts gradual improvements in the conditions of exploitation as a valid (or necessary) path to abolition. (See also Humane washing and Vegan washing, section 6.)
In anthropology, the principle of understanding each practice within the culture where it exists; in ethics, the thesis that a practice is right if the culture that performs it accepts it.
com: The first sense, associated with the anthropologist Franz Boas, is a valuable method: it helps us understand a practice before judging it and avoids mistaking one's own custom for everyone's standard. The second is a form of moral relativism and inherits its problems, because it would make any accepted practice, however cruel, immune to criticism. In the debate about animals, both traps appear: using culture to shield rodeos, bullfighting or Brazil's vaquejada, and condemning other peoples' practices while accepting those of one's own culture, like someone outraged at dog eating in another country who eats pigs at home. See Moral relativism, Double standard and Instrumentalization.

def: The position that right and wrong are not universal, but depend on the culture, era or person judging.
com: Two theses need separating. The first is descriptive and true: cultures and people disagree about what is right. The second is relativism proper: there would be no standard for saying some of these views are better than others. It faces well-known objections, such as those of the philosopher James Rachels: if it were true, we couldn't condemn slavery where it was accepted, nor speak of moral progress, and reformers would always be wrong. Some also invoke relativism selectively, only for the practices they want to protect. Some philosophers, such as Gilbert Harman and David Wong, defend more sophisticated versions, and the debate continues. Even in those versions, an animal's suffering isn't a matter of opinion: they feel pain whatever the culture of the observer. See Cultural relativism, Moral progress, Moral universality and Double standard.

def: The surgical amputation of part of an animal's ears (common in some dog breeds) for aesthetic reasons.
com: The cut is made on puppies of breeds such as Dobermann, pit bull and Great Dane, so that the ears stand erect, and it requires weeks of bandaging and splints. It is banned for cosmetic purposes in much of Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia and, in Brazil, by the Federal Council of Veterinary Medicine since 2008, but it is still legal in much of the United States. See Tail docking, Devocalization and Pedigree.

def: An enzyme extracted from the stomach of young calves, lambs or kids, used in traditional cheese production to coagulate milk.
com: Traditional rennet comes from the stomachs of calves, and also of lambs and kids, killed while young, which is why many cheeses are not even vegetarian. Today most industrial cheese in the United States and the United Kingdom uses chymosin produced by fermentation with microorganisms, but protected traditional cheeses such as Parmigiano Reggiano still require animal rennet. Labels do not always state where the rennet comes from. See Cheese, Dairy products and Vegetarianism.
